segments.t: Refusing to visit the agency while his father Mathias is there, Hippolyte asks Camille to meet him at a cafe. Sitting outside on a cold Paris afternoon, the two half-siblings sign contracts, talk about their shared father, and invent a warm new friendship. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Mon père est là?
Oui.
Je ne viens pas, alors. Je ne veux pas le voir.
On peut se retrouver ailleurs?
Salut!
Un café, s'il vous plaît.
D'accord.
Il a soudainement fait froid. C'est l'enfer en scooter.
Il gèle à vélo. Je pédale comme une folle!
Voici tes contrats.
Je suis désolée.
C'est mon père qui devrait s'excuser, pas toi.
Notre père! C'est trop bizarre.
On va juste oublier ça et devenir amis.
Tu es ma sœpote et je suis ton frote!
Tchin, frote!
Camille and Hippolyte break the ice. Let us examine their lines together.
Mon père est là?
'Is my father there?' The final word means 'there'. With rising intonation, the ordinary statement 'my father is there' becomes a question about Mathias's location.
Oui.
'Yes.' One word supplies the entire affirmative answer. Nothing needs to be repeated because the question already names her father and his location.
Je ne viens pas, alors. Je ne veux pas le voir.
'I am not coming, then. I do not want to see him.' The first negative denies coming. The second denies wanting to see him. The small object before 'see' refers back to his father.
On peut se retrouver ailleurs?
'Can we meet somewhere else?' The final word means 'elsewhere'. The action in the middle means meeting up, so Camille proposes a different place rather than cancelling.
Salut!
'Hi!' This familiar greeting can mean hello or goodbye. Here it opens their meeting, so it means 'hi'.
Un café, s'il vous plaît.
'A coffee, please.' French orders coffee by naming the drink with 'a'. The fixed ending adds 'please' politely, suitable for speaking to a waiter.
D'accord.
'All right.' The reply is an everyday 'okay'. The small attached word at the beginning belongs to the whole expression, rather than naming a separate object.
Il a soudainement fait froid. C'est l'enfer en scooter.
'It suddenly got cold. It is hell on a scooter.' The first sentence describes a sudden change in the weather. The second calls travel by scooter 'hell', an exaggerated description of the cold.
Il gèle à vélo. Je pédale comme une folle!
'It is freezing on a bike. I pedal like crazy!' The opening weather statement means it is freezing. The comparison after 'I pedal' literally says 'like a crazy woman', matching Camille.
Voici tes contrats.
'Here are your contracts.' The first word presents something: 'here are'. The plural word for 'your' belongs to the contracts, while addressing one person familiarly.
Je suis désolée.
'I am sorry.' The final word has a feminine ending because Camille is speaking. This apology leads Hippolyte to say that their father should be the one apologizing.
C'est mon père qui devrait s'excuser, pas toi.

'My father is the one who should apologize, not you.' The beginning singles out his father as the person who should apologize. The last two words mean 'not you', explicitly releasing Camille from blame.
Notre père! C'est trop bizarre.
'Our father! It is so weird.' Camille changes 'my' to 'our'. That single possessive acknowledges they share a father. The later word means 'too' or, here, emphatically 'so'.
On va juste oublier ça et devenir amis.

'We are just going to forget about that and become friends.' The opening 'we are going' introduces their plan. The two later actions mean 'forget' and 'become': leave the confusion behind and become friends.
Tu es ma sœpote et je suis ton frote!

'You are my sister-buddy and I am your brother-buddy!' These two invented nicknames blend the French words for sister or brother with the slang word for buddy. They are playful family-specific names, not standard vocabulary.
Tchin, frote!

'Cheers, brother-buddy!' The opening is a toast, like 'cheers'. Camille then uses their newly invented word for her brother who will also be her friend. Now listen to their cafe conversation once more from start to finish.
Mon père est là?
Oui.
Je ne viens pas, alors. Je ne veux pas le voir.
On peut se retrouver ailleurs?
Salut!
Un café, s'il vous plaît.
D'accord.
Il a soudainement fait froid. C'est l'enfer en scooter.
Il gèle à vélo. Je pédale comme une folle!
Voici tes contrats.
Je suis désolée.
C'est mon père qui devrait s'excuser, pas toi.
Notre père! C'est trop bizarre.
On va juste oublier ça et devenir amis.
Tu es ma sœpote et je suis ton frote!
Tchin, frote!
Having made peace with their unusual family bond, Camille and Hippolyte raise their cups together. Here is our final toast. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
